rows.question: How did our carriers' on-time performance change in Q3, especially on reefer?
rows.answer: Overall on-time pickup fell to 93.1% from 95.4% in Q2, and on-time delivery fell to 91.8% from 94.0% [1]. Reefer was the weakest mode, with on-time delivery down to 87.2% from 92.5%, which the scorecard attributes to the September hurricane disruption and longer produce dwell times [2]. Reefer reliability also slipped on the carrier side: carrier fall-offs rose to 4.4% of reefer loads from 2.1% in Q2 [3]. The Southeast reefer market memo adds context: Hurricane Corinne stranded about 1,100 refrigerated trailers in mid-September [4], and Ridgeline's reefer tender acceptance fell to 78% in September, pushing more produce loads to the spot market at higher cost [5]. Ridgeline paid $41,800 in produce detention in September, up from $23,500 in June, and only 62% was billed back to shippers [6][7].
rows.correctness_reason: The performance and reefer figures are correct, but the brief omits that 37 carriers were removed from the approved list, mostly for lapsed insurance.

rows.question: How much have Southeast diesel prices moved since July, and roughly what does that add to our fuel surcharge per mile?
rows.answer: Southeast retail on-highway diesel rose 31 cents per gallon, from $3.63 at the start of July to $3.94 in the week of October 6, 2026, an increase of about 8.5% [1]. The source's rule of thumb for a typical broker fuel surcharge table is one cent per mile for every six-cent rise in diesel, which puts the 31-cent move at roughly five cents more per mile in surcharge [2]. The Q3 Ridgeline memo gives no diesel or surcharge figures, but it does recommend adding a separate reefer fuel surcharge line for produce accounts [3].
rows.correctness_reason: The diesel increase and surcharge estimate are correct, but the brief omits the reference’s reefer consumption figure of about 0.8 gallons per hour.

rows.question: Summarize the broker transparency rule and what Ridgeline must change.
rows.answer: The broker transparency rule requires a property broker to keep an electronic record of every brokered transaction for at least three years, and that record must show the shipper's payment to the broker, the broker's payment to the carrier, and accessorial charges [1][2]. When a carrier or shipper party to a transaction requests the record, the broker must deliver it electronically within 48 hours [3]. For Ridgeline, this means the TMS must hold both shipper and carrier payment amounts on the same load record, a request process must be built to meet the 48-hour deadline, and carrier contracts can no longer contain clauses waiving the carrier's right to see the transaction record [4][5]. The rule does not require temperature records, though some receivers may demand reefer logs by contract [6].
rows.correctness_reason: The brief correctly states the recordkeeping, disclosure, waiver, and operational requirements, but omits the effective dates and fines of up to $10,000 per violation.

rows.question: Under the food traceability requirement, what do we as a broker have to keep or provide on produce loads?
rows.answer: Per the one traceability source in the library, a broker that only transports produce is not required to keep traceability lot codes, but must be able to provide shipping documents within 24 hours when a shipper or receiver requests them during a recall [1]. The shipper and receiver carry the record-keeping duty for key data elements such as lot code, quantity, and origin and destination [2]. Temperature logs are not a rule requirement, though many receivers now ask for them as a contract condition, so Ridgeline should check its shipper and receiver contracts for that [3].
rows.correctness_reason: The brief correctly states the broker’s obligations and temperature-log distinction, but omits the reference’s examples of covered foods.

rows.question: What did the fall carrier survey say about reefer carriers shrinking or leaving the market, and why?
rows.answer: The Mid-South Carrier Pulse Survey (Fall 2026) found reefer carriers are net shrinking: 22% plan to cut fleet size within six months and 9% are considering leaving reefer for dry van, while only 11% plan to add trucks [1][2]. Carriers planning to shrink most often cited insurance premiums, equipment financing costs, and unpaid detention time, and Forty-one percent of reefer carriers said they refuse loads from at least one shipper over chronic detention [3][4]. Ridgeline's own Q3 market memo reports the Southeast lost about 6% of small reefer fleets since January, mostly owner-operators with one to five trucks, though it gives no cause for those exits, and load-to-truck ratios hit 11.4 to 1 [5][6]. For Ridgeline, the detention findings point to shipper-side detention terms and billing as a lever on carrier retention, which the survey links to the reefer capacity squeeze [3][4].
rows.correctness_reason: The answer and findings correctly state all fleet plans and the three reasons for shrinking, including their percentages.

rows.question: What general rate increases are LTL carriers planning for 2027?
rows.answer: One industry outlook reports that five of the largest LTL carriers have announced early-2027 general rate increases ranging from 4.9% to 6.5%, with a median of 5.9% [1]. For Ridgeline, the bigger exposure may be accessorials, which the same outlook says are rising faster than base rates, with liftgate fees up about 9% on average and two carriers adding a residential delivery surcharge [2]. Shippers tendering fewer than 50 LTL shipments a month usually absorb the full GRI, while larger shippers typically negotiate it down by one to three points [3], so Ridgeline's shipper pricing should separate high-volume and low-volume accounts.
rows.correctness_reason: The brief correctly states the GRI range and median, accessorial increases, and the different impacts on smaller and larger shippers.

rows.question: What's driving reefer spot rates out of the Southeast this quarter, and what does it mean for our produce shippers?
rows.answer: Q3 Southeast reefer spot averaged $2.87 per mile, up 14% from Q2 [1]. The drivers cited were a Georgia and Florida produce push that ran three weeks long [2], Hurricane Corinne closing the Port of Savannah for four days and stranding about 1,100 reefer trailers [3], and a 6% loss of small reefer fleets since January [4], with diesel at $3.94 a gallon adding cost [10]. For Ridgeline's produce shippers, spring contract rates are now well below market [5], and growers say freight is their top cost surprise [6]. Carrier exit pressure is real: 22% of reefer carriers plan to shrink [7], detention is a leading reason [8], and Forty-one percent of reefer carriers refuse loads from at least one shipper over detention [9], so detention handling is a likely lever for keeping capacity on Ridgeline's produce lanes [9]. Reefer service has also slipped, with on-time delivery down to 87.2% and carrier fall-off up to 4.4% in Q3 [11][12].
rows.correctness_reason: The brief correctly states the rate increase and three main drivers, but omits the 78% tender acceptance rate, the shift to spot, and the recommended contract, fuel surcharge, and advance-booking actions.

rows.question: Which of our produce shippers are driving detention costs, and how much are we paying?
rows.answer: In September 2026 Ridgeline paid $41,800 in detention on produce loads, up from $23,500 in June [1]. Under policy carriers get 2 free hours, then $75 per hour capped at $600 per stop [2]. ($7,900, 3.9 hours) and Gator Grove Citrus ($5,150, 3.4 hours) [3][4][5][6]. Only 62% of produce detention was billed back to shippers, because the rest lacked signed in and out times on the BOL [7], and the Q3 carrier scorecard ties longer produce dwell to weaker reefer on-time delivery [8].
rows.correctness_reason: The answer and findings together correctly state the detention totals, all three shippers’ costs and dwell times, their 58% share, and the 62% billback rate and cause.
